I can prove a new universal single-use allocation, and use it to prove your exact target for an all-phase subclass:The requested allocation holds if every positive U source has width six and all but at most one have equal leg heights.The exceptional positive source may have arbitrary independent even leg heights. All negative U sources retain arbitrary allowed widths, independent heights, phases and isometries; all rotor sources remain unrestricted.In particular, it holds with one positive  $U(6,a,b)$  and arbitrarily many negative U sources and rotors.The unrestricted case—with arbitrary positive widths and independently unequal positive legs—remains open in this answer. I have neither a proof nor a complete feasible counterexample for that case.The new general step is stronger than an event-only estimate: it pays every activated original positive tip and every blank-gate marked side jointly with  $B_U+B_R$ . Its proof uses a finite directed routing argument through complete zero-rotor supports, with distinct terminal payments.1. The new universal allocationCall an original  $1P2T$  singleton occurrence activated when at least one of its two original intratile selections belongs to the final  $P$ .Define: $A_+$ : the number of activated original positive-U terminal singleton occurrences; $G_b$ : the number of marked canonical sides whose gate is finally blank.There are exactly two original positive terminal singleton occurrences per positive U. We count occurrences with their original ownership, even when two occur in the same physical tile.Support-routing theoremFor every finite complete feasible fusion in the full source class,
$$\boxed{
B_U+B_R+A_++G_b\ \le\ 2B_{11}+\Lambda.
}
\tag{6}$$
This includes activated positive tips unrelated to a marked side. If a blank-gate marked side also has its positive tip activated, both contributions are legitimate: the proof below gives them disjoint payments.Put
$$\mathcal R=S+C-K_{\mathrm{irregular}}.$$
Your exact identity gives
$$2\mathcal R=2B_{11}-B_U-B_R+\Lambda.$$
Consequently, (6) implies
$$\boxed{
\mathcal R\ge
\left\lceil\frac{A_++G_b}{2}\right\rceil.
}
\tag{7}$$
In particular,
$$\boxed{K_{\mathrm{irregular}}\le S+C}
\tag{8}$$
holds universally, with arbitrary U and rotor phases.The resulting bound for the precise budget in your question is
$$\boxed{
N+S+C-K_{\mathrm{irregular}}-G
\ \ge\
N-G+\left\lceil\frac{A_++G_b}{2}\right\rceil.
}
\tag{9}$$
Thus all fusions with  $G=0$  satisfy reserve, without a restriction on the zero-rotor phases or on  $B_R$ . Equation (6), however, also carries actual marked-side costs; it is not merely an event-only subclass.I take the source catalogue, half-slot identities, marked-side injection and positive-side rotor barrier in your supplied notes as established inputs. The new parts are the support bridge, routing injection, disjoint blank-gate payment, and the gate geometry used below.2. A zero-rotor triple activates a uniquely paired regular singletonNormalize a zero-charge rotor with three-endpoint tiles to
$$R_A=R_+(-3,0).$$
One of its original  $3P0T$  tiles is
$$Q=\{0,1\}\times\{2,3\},$$
with endpoints
$$(0,2),(0,3),(1,3)$$
and missing corner
$$p=(1,2).$$
Pair it with this rotor’s original regular singleton tile
$$Q'=\{0,1\}\times\{0,1\}.$$
Its endpoint and selections are
$$q=(0,1),\qquad (0,0),(1,1).$$
If  $p\in P$ , the old selection
$$x=(1,1)$$
has two persistent endpoint neighbors:  $q$  and  $p$ . Complete retained-support feasibility therefore forces  $x\in P$ . Hence the paired regular singleton is activated.The tiling-preserving half-turn
$$(r,c)\longmapsto(-1-r,5-c)$$
gives the rotor’s second triple/singleton pairing. The two pairings are disjoint and exhaust its two triples and two regular singletons. Tiling-preserving rotations, reflections and translations cover every zero-charge rotor having  $3P0T$  groups.We have therefore proved an all-placement statement:Each zero-rotor original triple has a uniquely paired original regular singleton. Filling the triple’s missing corner activates that singleton, and the pairing is bijective within the source.This deduction uses the complete support list. When it forces an old selection into  $P$ , the fixed-union hypothesis supplies its foreign original endpoint owner and original matching edge. No endpoint is created by reclassification.3. The payment lemma for activated regular singletonsFor a physical tile  $Q$ , let  $d_Q$  count its activated original regular singleton occurrences.Except in the forwarding case described below,
$$d_Q\le \Lambda_Q.
\tag{10}$$
The possibilities are:Final tile containing an activated original  $1P2T$  singletonAvailable  $\Lambda_Q$ UseNonfull, two endpoints $1$ Pay its one activated regular singletonNonfull, three endpoints $2$ Pay its one activated regular singletonFull  $2+1+1$ Number of original regular singletonsPay each such occurrence separatelyFull four-singleton tileNumber of original regular singletonsPay each such occurrence separatelyFull  $3+1$ , singleton regular $0$ Forward through the triple ownerHere is why the nonfull cases have the stated form.Suppose  $q$  was an original regular singleton. Both its original intratile selections remain occupied.If the final tile has two endpoints, exactly one of those selections has become an endpoint. The other remains selected, forcing the fourth corner blank. The new endpoint is an inactive irregular singleton: its sole adjacent original blank is that finally blank fourth corner. Thus
$$i_Q=1,\qquad k_Q=c_Q=0,\qquad \Lambda_Q=1.$$
If the final tile has three endpoints,  $q$  must be the elbow of the L. Its two original selections have both become endpoints. The two leaves cannot be a common original pair, because they are diagonal. Each is an inactive irregular singleton, with the missing corner as its original blank. Thus
$$i_Q=2,\qquad k_Q=c_Q=0,\qquad \Lambda_Q=2.$$
For the full tiles, the last three lines follow directly from your accepted half-slot table:in  $2+1+1$ ,  $\Lambda_Q=2-q$ , exactly the number of regular singletons;in four-singleton tiles,  $\Lambda_Q=4-q$ , again that number;a  $3+1$  tile with a regular singleton has  $\Lambda_Q=0$ .The distinction between regular and irregular singleton activation matters. An activated irregular singleton need not have a positive local  $\Lambda_Q$ ; the routing theorem uses regular singletons.4. Finite routing pays  $B_R$  and every activated positive tipUse original regular singleton occurrences as vertices. Start one token at:the paired regular singleton of every actual  $B_R$  triple;every activated positive terminal singleton counted in  $A_+$ .All starting vertices are activated.At an activated regular singleton, apply the following rule.If its tile is an ordinary payment case in the preceding table, terminate and use one unit of that tile’s  $\Lambda_Q$ .If its tile is full  $3+1$  and the triple belongs to a phase- $(1,1)$  U source, terminate at that original U triple.If its tile is full  $3+1$  and the triple belongs to a zero rotor, move to that triple’s uniquely paired regular singleton.The support bridge proves that every successor is activated.Why the paths cannot merge or cycleEvery zero-rotor target vertex has at most one predecessor. Its paired triple is fixed, and a predecessor must be the unique original regular singleton occupying that triple tile’s fourth corner.Every starting vertex has indegree zero:a positive singleton can never be the paired singleton of a zero rotor;a  $B_R$  starting vertex is paired with a triple whose fourth-corner owner is irregular, whereas an incoming routing edge requires that owner to be regular.These facts exclude both mergers and cycles reachable from a starting vertex. A merger would contradict unique predecessors. A path entering a cycle would either give its entry vertex two predecessors or place its indegree-zero root on the cycle.The source family is finite, so every starting path terminates.Why the terminal payments are distinctDifferent terminal occurrences in one physical payment tile use different units from  $d_Q\le\Lambda_Q$ . This permits several paths to end in the same tile without spending one unit twice.A U-triple terminal has a regular singleton in its fourth corner. It therefore cannot be one of the U triples counted in  $B_U$ , whose singleton is irregular. Different paths cannot terminate at the same U triple, because that triple has only one fourth-corner owner.Each phase- $(1,1)$  U has exactly two original triples. After reserving the  $B_U$  units, at most
$$2B_{11}-B_U$$
remain for routing terminals. Hence
$$B_R+A_+
\le \Lambda+2B_{11}-B_U.
\tag{11}$$
This proves the universal event-and-activation allocation. It does not assume the pending rotor-only finite-descent theorem. In particular, it does not spend any separate rectangle Euler credit in addition to  $\Lambda$ .5. Then
$$A_++G_b\ge G-1.$$

After the explicit routing, the remaining total capacity is an even integer; when rounding supplies an additional unit, at least one actual unused unit remains among the U-triple and  $\Lambda$  capacities.A dimension condition for arbitrary positive widthsThe same proof extends beyond width six.Let  $W$  be the maximum positive U width. Assume:Every phase- $01$  and phase- $11$  U source has width at least  $W$ .Both leg heights of each such source are at least  $W-2$ .Every positive U has equal leg heights, except possibly one positive source.Phase- $10$  dimensions and all rotor phases remain unrestricted.For a positive width  $w\le W$ , these conditions ensure that a phase- $01$  bar or near leg, or a horizontal phase- $11$  stem, reaches its opposite positive leg and is excluded. A vertical phase- $11$  bar also reaches that opposite leg; clearing it activates the corresponding positive tip on equal-leg sources, and the shorter tip on an unequal source.For completeness, phase- $10$  tip activation works for arbitrary positive widths. Its downward orientation must clear the same positive leg. In its rightward orientation, its upward bar would meet the positive upper bar unless it lies beyond the positive width; in that latter case its stem crosses the opposite positive leg. Thus only the activating downward orientation survives.The preceding allocation and parity proof therefore apply unchanged. At  $W=6$ , the two size conditions on negative sources are automatic.8. An inward phase- $11$  tip can carry an obligation through its regular stem toward its bar cap. These are real complete-support obligations, but they do not yet provide a globally disjoint additional payment.The collision with existing payment is precise. An activated irregular singleton may lie in a full exceptional  $3+1$  tile with
$$i_Q=1,\qquad k_Q=1,\qquad c_Q=0,\qquad b_Q=1,\qquad\Lambda_Q=0.$$
That contact is already counted in  $B_U$  or  $B_R$ . If a marked-side obligation is sent through the same zero-rotor companion route, it attempts to use the event’s route a second time. The regular-singleton injection proved above does not authorize that duplication.Complete supports can propagate the obligation farther along a U leg or bar. What is still missing is a global proof that these further paths terminate in distinct unused capacities, including when they turn, meet other caps, or reach a positive source. The local full-tile classification alone does not establish this. Nor does this local obstruction constitute a feasible counterexample.Necessary form of a counterexampleEquation (9) supplies a sharper obstruction than the previous slot bound. Any violation must satisfy
$$\boxed{
2G-A_+-G_b\ge2N+2.
}

Thus a counterexample with exactly one positive source would require positive width at least eight, as well as the complete support obligations above.Status of the three questionsThe results here have distinct scopes:Universal event reserve: proved,
$$K_{\mathrm{irregular}}\le S+C.$$
Your weaker joint allocation: proved for the all-phase classes in Sections 6–7; unresolved for unrestricted positive widths and leg heights.Stronger joint reserve: the argument does not prove
$$K_{\mathrm{irregular}}+G\le S+C$$
when  $G>0$ , and establishes no counterexample to it.Actual ambient slack: the established ledger gives  $\sigma\ge0$  in the proved subclasses. No failure of ambient  $\sigma\ge0$  is established.The new mathematical content is the universal allocation (6): exceptional zero-rotor contacts, all activated positive tips, and blank-gate marks have a finite, injective, single-use payment. It settles the stated target under the geometric conditions above while leaving the remaining U-cap clustering question explicit.
